newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU says UK breaks beef ban, mulls legal action.
newsitem.headline: EU says UK breaks beef ban, mulls legal action.

text.p: The European Commission is considering legal action against Britain for illegal exports of unspecified quantities of British beef to European Union and other countries, a Commission spokesman said on Wednesday.

The EU banned exports of British beef and beef products in March 1996 to protect consumer health after the British government said it was possible a human form of the fatal mad cow disease, CJD, could be caught from eating infected beef.
Despite a barrage of questioning, the spokesman declined to give details about how much beef was exported and to which countries, saying this would hinder legal inquiries.
In a brief statement the EU's executive would only say that an EU inspection mission's report "confirmed suspicions" of fraudulent exports to some member states and non-EU countries.
"The Commission is examining if the evident inefficiency of controls should result in infringement proceedings," it added.
EU sources said British beef was allegedly illegally exported to Spain and to two non-EU countries.
But another source, who had participated at the weekly meeting of EU Commissioners, said British beef had been illegally exported to France via Belgium.
The Commission's announcement followed an EU veterinary inspectors' mission last week to Britain, which included visits to sea ports, and pressure from European Parliament members.

The announcement coincided with a hearing of British government and farmers' complaints to the European Court of Justice in Luxembourg that the Commission had overstepped its powers in imposing the worldwide ban on British beef exports.
The Court is due to issue a final ruling at the end of 1997.
In the statement, the EU's food safety, agriculture and anti-fraud commissioners, Emma Bonino, Franz Fischler and Anita Gradin, urged the 15 member states to reinforce controls on beef imports.
The Commission said it would provide all necessary support to combat the fraud. In the statement, Bonino also urged Britain to respect the beef export ban.
Commission sources said the statement was intended to avoid any allegation of a cover-up, although for legal reasons no details could be given at this stage.
"The Commission considers that it must inform consumers and show that it is enforcing controls," explained one source.
British officials declined to give details.
"We are taking the allegations very seriously and will investigate them thoroughly," said one, adding that British sea ports had been closely monitored.

The official said that since the EU beef ban was imposed 16 months ago, some 14,000 checks had carried out in British ports, including 1,590 in the week leading up to the EU inspectors' latest report.
In July 1996, EU Commission President Jacques Santer dismissed media allegations that British beef had been fraudulently exported to Italy and other continental countries.
